McCoy’s Lab

Health monitoring for astronauts, Star Trek style.

Team USS Enterprise NASA Space Apps 2026 Sickbay · Dr. Leonard McCoy
Challenge #4 — Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions.
Slide 02 · The Problem

On a long mission, there is no doctor on board

NASA’s Human Research Program names five hazards of human spaceflight — and the crew member is the first line of defence against every one of them.

Hazard 01Radiation
Hazard 02Isolation & Confinement
Hazard 03Distance from Earth
Hazard 04Gravity Fields
Hazard 05Hostile, Closed Environments

Track

An astronaut needs to track their own health, over time — not just in a single check-up.

Notice

They need to see, at a glance, when something starts to look off.

Act

And they need to know what to do first — in plain language, on the spot.

Source: NASA Human Research Program — The 5 Hazards of Human Spaceflight

Slide 03 · The App

What McCoy’s Lab does

01

Tracks resting heart rate over time

One number per vital on the welcome screen, with the trend behind it — the latest reading, “your normal”, and the last 10 readings on a chart.

02

Links it to sleep and recovery

Heart rate sits alongside sleep, body temperature, blood pressure, oxygenation and blood sugar, so recovery is part of the same picture.

03

Checks in on mood, too

No sensor can read a mood, so the astronaut logs it: a five-face check-in at the top of the chart box, in a controls row above the chart title — mood on the left, a compact “Measure now” button on the right. Tap a face, from 1 (low) to 5 (great), and the centre chart switches to mood. Nothing sits below the chart.

04

Says what to do first

When a reading looks off, clear rest-and-re-measure guidance — first on the space station, then on the spacecraft.

05

Two cards below the chart

McCoy’s Note turns the live readings into a one-line doctor’s verdict. Beside it, the Stardate card shows the current stardate and the signal delay to Earth.

Slide 04 · How It Works

Measure. Compare. Alert.

Step 1 · Sense

Every 15 seconds

A simulated sensor measures resting heart rate — 68–78 bpm in the demo — plus on-demand “Measure now” at any time.

Step 2 · Baseline

“Your normal”

The average of resting readings. Resting means below 80 bpm — the baseline the trend is judged against.

Step 3 · Alert

Over 100 bpm

Triggers “Elevated heart rate alert”: rest and measure again. If it stays high, seek medical care.

Limits <80 / >100 bpm = prototype design choices Not NASA-published ranges All readings labelled simulated
Slide 05 · The Interface

Two environments, one flow

  • Pure-CSS LCARS. TNG colour blocks and curved frames, Antonio font, uppercase labels — no images, no library.
  • Layout. Six vital tiles in a column on the left, readings on a big centre screen. Inside the chart box, a controls row at the top — above the chart title — holds the five-face mood check-in on the left and a compact “Measure now” button on the right; nothing sits below the chart. Responsive down to phone width.
  • Frame closes at the bottom. A footer bar finishes the LCARS frame, with mirrored elbow corners at the bottom-left and bottom-right.
  • Ship card at the top. Next to the title sits a card in the same style as the side tiles: USS Enterprise · NCC-1701-D, Chief Medical Officer · Dr. Leonard McCoy, Sickbay · Day 1 or 2 — plus the Space Station / Spacecraft toggle that switches the environment.
  • Click a tile, switch the chart. Heart rate is the live series; sleep, temperature, blood pressure, oxygenation and blood sugar are labelled simulated series. Tapping a face on the mood strip switches the chart to mood instead.
  • The chart is pure SVG. Aqua line, orange dots, value labels above each point, gridlines at each y-label — heart rate scaled 60–110 bpm with a dashed red line at the 100 bpm threshold.
Slide 06 · Live Verification

What we verified live

Not a mock-up: a FastAPI back end and a simulated sensor, running end to end during the demo.

  • ✓ Three endpoints, all exercised. GET /readings serves the readings; POST /measure adds one on demand; POST /mood logs a mood check-in.
  • ✓ The movement is visible. The sensor thread adds a reading every 15 seconds and the front polls every 15 seconds.
  • ✓ The alert fires — and only when it should. “Measure now” adds 105 bpm and the alert appears; in normal readings, it stays off.
  • ✓ Every chart keeps moving. The same pipeline updates temperature (36.4–36.7 °C), systolic pressure (118–122), oxygenation (97–99%) and blood sugar (90–110 mg/dL) every 15 seconds. Sleep stays a 7-night series — it changes nightly, not minutely.
  • ✓ Mood is logged by hand — because it has to be. Mood cannot come from a sensor, so the astronaut taps a face on the check-in strip and the front sends it with POST /mood; the centre chart switches to the mood series.
  • ! The demo never breaks. If the back end is down, the front falls back locally and keeps running.
Slide 07 · Why It Matters

The crew member sees the trend, not clutter

One number per tile. One alert. One chart.

Built in · McCoy’s Note

The app interprets, not just displays: McCoy’s Note turns the live readings into a one-line doctor’s verdict, right below the chart.
